name: Ranger Gloves
what_it_is: Simple full-finger trail gloves with a thin neoprene cuff, a soft wipe-friendly thumb and touchscreen fingertips.
good_for: A cheap first pair of gloves. They protect your hands in small crashes and help your grip when your hands get sweaty.
watch_out: No padding, so long rough days can be harder on your palms.
our_take: A no-fuss first pair. Cheap enough that you won't mind wrecking them.

name: Nomad 2 MIPS Helmet
what_it_is: An open-face trail helmet with MIPS (a layer that helps with twisting forces in a crash), a dial to adjust the fit and a removable visor. 320g in M/L.
good_for: A first proper MTB helmet that doesn't cost a lot but still has MIPS.
watch_out: The listing we checked only mentions the US safety standard. Make sure the one you buy has the AS/NZS 2063 sticker inside, which Australian law needs for road riding.
our_take: The best-value MIPS helmet we found for a first MTB lid. Just check for the Aussie sticker.

name: Speedframe MIPS Helmet
what_it_is: A trail helmet with more coverage at the back, MIPS, a 360-degree fit system and a visor that moves up so goggles fit underneath. Certified to AS/NZS 2063.
good_for: Riders who are getting faster and want more coverage and a visor that works with goggles.
watch_out: It's about $40 more than the Bell Nomad 2 for similar features, so it's best bought on sale.
our_take: Great coverage and goggle-friendly. Wait for a sale and it's a top pick.

name: Sanction 2 Full Face Helmet
what_it_is: A budget full-face helmet with a chin bar, 14 vents and removable washable cheek pads. Certified to the ASTM downhill standard. 1040g in M.
good_for: Downhill races and bike park days, where a full-face helmet is the norm.
watch_out: It's hot on long climbs. The listing doesn't mention AS/NZS 2063, so check the sticker before you buy.
our_take: The cheapest sensible way into a full-face helmet for downhill and park days.

name: Launch D3O Knee Guards
what_it_is: Slip-on knee pads with soft CE-certified D3O padding that hardens when you hit something. They have padded sides and breathable fabric.
good_for: Everyday trail riding and racing. They're comfy enough to pedal in all day.
watch_out: Pull-on pads mean taking your shoes off to put them on. Try them on in store to get the size right.
our_take: Comfy enough to forget you're wearing them. Our pick for everyday knee pads.

name: Launch Pro Knee Guards
what_it_is: Heavier-duty knee guards with CE D3O padding, a tough skid plate and a hard cap that you can remove.
good_for: Downhill, enduro and bike park riding where crashes are faster and harder.
watch_out: They're bulkier and warmer than the standard Launch. The $123 price was a clearance price when we checked.
our_take: Proper armour for downhill. Overkill for normal trail rides.

name: Composite Flat Pedals
what_it_is: Light nylon flat pedals (355g a pair) with a big 115 x 105mm platform and 10 replaceable pins per side.
good_for: Swapping out the plastic pedals a new bike comes with. A big, grippy platform makes a huge difference for beginners.
watch_out: The plastic body will wear on rocks over time. That's normal at this price.
our_take: The single best cheap upgrade for a new bike. Grippy, light and wide.

name: Aluminium Flat Pedals
what_it_is: Thin aluminium flat pedals (386g a pair) with the same big platform as the composite version and a steel axle. Comes with spare pins.
good_for: Riders who smash pedals on rocks and want something tougher and thinner.
watch_out: It's three times the price of the composite version for similar grip. Most riders won't need the upgrade.
our_take: Brilliant pedals, but the composite version is most of the way there for a third of the price.

name: Freerider Flat Shoes
what_it_is: Flat-pedal shoes with Five Ten's sticky Stealth rubber sole, which grips pedal pins really well. The upper is leather and textile.
good_for: Anyone riding flat pedals. Sticky shoes are one of the best upgrades for confidence on rough ground.
watch_out: They're not waterproof, and the soft rubber wears faster if you walk a lot.
our_take: Sticky shoes plus pinned pedals is a huge confidence boost. A classic for a reason.

name: Minion DHF 29 x 2.5 (3C EXO TR)
what_it_is: One of the most popular front tyres in mountain biking. It has big cornering knobs, a soft grippy rubber and a tubeless-ready folding bead.
good_for: A front tyre upgrade for trail, enduro and downhill. It grips well on loose SA dirt.
watch_out: Check your wheel size first (29 or 27.5 inch). The $65 price was a clearance price when we checked.
our_take: The default front tyre for loose, dry trails like ours. Grab it on sale.

name: Mini M.U.L.E. 1.5L (Kids)
what_it_is: A small hydration pack made for kids. It holds a 1.5L water bladder and has a pocket for a tool and a safety whistle on the chest strap.
good_for: Young riders on longer rides and race days, so they keep drinking without stopping.
watch_out: 1.5L is plenty for kids but not for adults on long hot rides.
our_take: Sized right for kids, so they actually drink on race day.

name: M.U.L.E. 8 (3L)
what_it_is: A hydration pack with a 3L bladder in its own insulated sleeve and 8L of storage. It's made from tough Cordura fabric.
good_for: Long hot SA summer rides where 3L of cool water matters.
watch_out: This is the heavy-duty Mil Spec version, so a lighter riding pack can do the job for less.
our_take: Built to last forever, and that 3L matters in an SA summer. Heavier than it needs to be, though.

name: Big.Nine 80
what_it_is: An aluminium 29er hardtail with a 100mm RockShox Judy coil fork (with lockout), a Shimano CUES 1x9 drivetrain and Shimano hydraulic disc brakes.
good_for: A first proper mountain bike for club races and trail riding. Hydraulic brakes and a name-brand fork are rare at this price.
watch_out: It was pre-order only when we checked, with most sizes sold out. There is no dropper post, and the wire-bead tyres are worth upgrading later.
our_take: Our pick for a first race bike under $1,000. The fork and brakes are a step above most bikes at this price.

name: Talon 2
what_it_is: An aluminium hardtail with a 100mm coil fork on the 29er sizes, a 1x9 drivetrain with a clutch derailleur, Tektro hydraulic disc brakes and tubeless-compatible rims. Smaller sizes use 27.5 inch wheels.
good_for: Younger or smaller riders, because it comes in sizes from XS with 27.5 inch wheels, and riders who want to buy from a local Giant shop.
watch_out: This is the recommended retail price, and you buy it through a Giant dealer. The tyres are wire bead, so going tubeless will need new tyres.
our_take: A safe all-rounder with sizes for kids through to adults. A good choice when you want a local shop to look after it.

name: Elite Pro Lock-On Grips 135mm
what_it_is: Soft rubber grips that bolt onto the bars with a single clamp, so they never twist or slip off.
good_for: Replacing worn or slippery stock grips. Lock-on grips also come off easily when you need to change brakes or shifters.
watch_out: Grips are personal. If you have small hands, look for a thinner grip.
our_take: A cheap way to make any bike feel nicer to hold. Lock-on is a must for MTB.

name: B05S Resin Brake Pads
what_it_is: Replacement resin (organic) disc brake pads for the Shimano two-piston brakes found on lots of beginner bikes, including the MT200 and MT400.
good_for: Keeping a spare set at home. Worn pads are one of the most common reasons a bike fails its check before a race.
watch_out: They only fit certain brakes, so check your brake model against the list on the shop page. Resin pads wear faster in wet, gritty conditions.
our_take: Cheap insurance. Every rider with Shimano brakes should have a spare pair.

name: No Puncture Hassle Tubeless Sealant 1L
what_it_is: Liquid that goes inside tubeless tyres and plugs holes up to 6mm as you ride. It glows under UV light so you can find punctures.
good_for: Riders running tubeless. SA trails are full of thorns and sharp rocks, and sealant fixes most small punctures without you stopping.
watch_out: Sealant dries out, so top it up every few months, more often in hot weather. A 1L bottle lasts a long time, so split it with a friend. Club 99 members paid $65 when we checked.
our_take: If you run tubeless, you need sealant. This one is easy to find in Australian shops.

name: Pocket Drive Pro HV Pump
what_it_is: A small aluminium hand pump (104g) made to push lots of air into big MTB tyres. It has a flexible hose, works on both valve types and comes with a frame mount.
good_for: Carrying on every ride or in the race-day bag, so a flat doesn't end your day.
watch_out: Hand pumps are slow compared with a floor pump at home. It can't seat a tubeless tyre from scratch.
our_take: Small, tough and quick for its size. A good "always in the pack" pump.

name: M19 Multi-Tool
what_it_is: A pocket tool (175g) with 19 functions, including the hex keys most bikes need, a chain breaker and spoke keys.
good_for: Fixing most trailside problems, like a loose bolt, a twisted seat or a broken chain.
watch_out: It was out of stock at Pushys when we checked, so look at other shops too. It's heavier than a basic tool without a chain breaker.
our_take: One of the most complete pocket tools around. Learn to use the chain tool before you need it.

name: V3 Dropper Post
what_it_is: A seat post that drops your saddle out of the way at the push of a lever, then pops back up for climbing. Comes in lots of lengths (90 to 240mm) and sizes, and the travel can be trimmed by up to 20mm.
good_for: Steep descents, enduro and anyone who wants more room to move on the bike. It's one of the biggest upgrades for confidence going downhill.
watch_out: The remote lever is sold separately. Check your frame's seat post size (like 30.9 or 31.6mm) and that it can run an internal cable before you buy.
our_take: A light, simple dropper with lots of drop for the money. Make sure you budget for the remote.
